# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
# Critical Reading: Varden County Cluster-Randomised Trial (VC-2023-04)

This is a much stronger study than the Halden pilot. It is randomised and stratified, the protocol was registered, output comes from administrative records, actual hours come from timesheets, and the authors explicitly reject the scheduled-hours figure as misleading. The arithmetic checks out:

| Check | Calculation | Reported |
|---|---|---|
| Case-processing actual hours | 33.0 / 37.9 = 0.871 | −13% ✓ |
| Counter actual hours | 31.2 / 37.6 = 0.830 | −17% ✓ |
| Case-processing output per hour | 0.979 / 0.87 = 1.125 | +12.5% ✓ |
| Counter output per hour | 0.886 / 0.83 = 1.067 | +6.7% ✓ |
| Case-processing vs scheduled hours | 0.979 / 0.80 = 1.224 | "22%" ✓ |

The conclusions are mostly well calibrated. A few issues remain, some of which bear directly on the headline findings.

## 1. Cost is never analysed, and case-processing probably did not pay for itself

The discussion says per-hour gains do not imply that the reduction "pays for itself," but the paper applies this only to counter offices. Case-processing staff worked about 3 hours a week of overtime beyond their 30 scheduled hours, and the timesheets record overtime *claimed*, which suggests it was paid.

A rough illustration (my assumptions, not the paper's figures):
- Full pay for 30 hours means the base hourly rate rises by 25%.
- Three overtime hours, at a typical 1.5× premium on that rate, would add roughly 15% to the wage bill.
- Output per FTE also fell by about 2%.

On those assumptions, labour cost per case closed rose by something like 15–18%. The true figure depends on the overtime terms, which the paper doesn't give. Even so, "little or no measurable loss of output per employee" is not the same as "no loss of service at no extra cost." The paper should report cost per unit of output.

## 2. The counter per-hour gain may be a queueing artefact

When the same demand is met with fewer staff present, queues lengthen and staff spend less time idle between contacts. Output per hour then rises mechanically through higher utilisation, even if nobody works any faster. The data fit this pattern: waits rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes and abandoned calls from 6% to 10%.

The paper calls this "somewhat more productive." It may instead be the same productivity with less slack. This is the clearest case where per-hour productivity and service quality move in opposite directions. Reporting idle or wrap-up time from the telephony system would help separate the two.

## 3. Backlogs are measurable but not reported

Case-processing output per FTE was held up partly by overtime "to clear backlogs." The limitations section worries that backlogs could build beyond statutory deadlines. The case-management system can measure this directly through queue size, inflow versus closures, and deadline compliance.

Without those figures, stable closures could hide a growing queue, or a one-off drawdown of an existing backlog. Either would make the 9-month result unrepresentative of a steady state.

## 4. Several outcomes are not reported as difference-in-differences

The design specifies difference-in-differences against the pre-period. Some registered secondary outcomes are not presented that way:

- **Waiting time** (a registered outcome): shown only as treated offices before and after (4.2 → 6.9), with no control trend and no confidence interval.
- **Abandoned calls** (6% → 10%): treated offices only, and not in the table.
- **Quality**: shown as "3.1% v 3.0%" and "11.8% v 10.9%." The paper doesn't say which figure is treated and which is control, these appear to be levels rather than difference-in-differences, and there is no interval. The counter repeat-contact rise of about 0.9 points could matter, because callers who abandon or are poorly served may come back.

The direction is probably right, but these departures from the registered analysis should be fixed or explained.

## 5. Sick days may fall partly by construction

The paper doesn't say whether the 30 hours were delivered as four days or as five shorter days. If staff work four days, the number of days on which anyone *could* be off sick falls by 20%. Sick days per FTE would then drop by roughly 20% at an unchanged illness rate.

Against that benchmark, the 29% fall would represent only about a 9–11% reduction in the underlying rate. The sick-day estimate also has no confidence interval. Sickness absence measured in hours, or per scheduled day, would resolve this.

## 6. Inference with few clusters

Standard errors are clustered by office, with 14 offices in one stratum and only 10 in the other. Conventional clustered standard errors tend to be too small with this few clusters. The counter per-hour interval (+0.4 to +13.3) only just excludes zero and could fail to do so under a small-sample correction such as a wild cluster bootstrap.

On the comparison between strata:
- The per-FTE difference (−2.1% vs −11.4%) looks robust: a rough difference test gives z ≈ 2.5.
- The per-hour difference (+12.5% vs +6.7%) has heavily overlapping intervals. "More modest" should not be read as a demonstrated difference between strata.

## 7. The meetings analysis is weaker than its correlation, and stronger than its correlation

The authors flag this analysis appropriately. Two further points apply.

**Weaker:** Meeting time was measured only in month six, with no pre-period. The 3.8 vs 7.1 hour gap could partly reflect differences that existed before the trial, so this is not a difference-in-differences. With n = 7, the 95% interval for r = 0.71 runs from roughly 0 to 0.95.

**Stronger:** The paper's own figures support the story more directly than the correlation does. Actual hours fell by 4.9 per week, and meetings were 3.3 hours lower. If that gap reflects real cuts, about two-thirds of the lost hours came out of meetings. Non-meeting time would have fallen only from about 30.8 to 29.2 hours, roughly 5%, while output fell 2%. That simple calculation suggests most of the per-hour gain could come from removing meetings rather than from working faster.

The registered 24-month confirmatory test is the right response. It should include baseline meeting data.

## 8. Scope of the counter finding

Treated counter offices kept their opening hours while each employee worked fewer hours. The result is therefore a test of *fewer staff on shift*, not of reduced hours in coverage work generally. Hiring to restore cover, shorter opening hours, or appointment systems could give different results. The paper's framing ("output tied to presence") is accurate, but readers should not take the −11.4% as fixed for every implementation.

The limitations section also notes that control staff knew about the trial. A control group that works harder to compete (John Henry effect) or loses morale (resentful demoralisation) could bias estimates in either direction. Neither is likely to explain the counter result, given the mechanical staffing effect.

## Bearing on the Halden pilot

This trial addresses most of the weaknesses I raised in the earlier paper and largely confirms them:

- **Scheduled vs actual hours:** Measuring against scheduled hours overstated the case-processing gain from 12.5% to 22%. Halden's 23.4% was computed the same way, so it is very likely overstated.
- **Coverage-bound work:** Under randomisation, counter output fell by about 11% and service worsened. This is consistent with Halden's retail output drop and its 50% retail reversion rate, and contradicts Halden's "sector-general" conclusion.
- **Mechanism:** The meetings evidence, though exploratory, favours the "forcing device" explanation that Halden's interviews pointed to over Halden's preferred fatigue explanation.

## Bottom line

**Well supported:**
- In backlog-type work, output per employee was roughly maintained.
- Output per actual hour rose by about 12%.
- Scheduled-hours calculations materially overstate productivity gains.
- In coverage-bound work implemented as fewer staff on shift, output and service fell.

**Needs qualification:**
- Case-processing results may have come with substantially higher cost per case because of paid overtime.
- The counter per-hour gain may reflect fuller utilisation rather than faster work.
- The sick-day reduction may be partly mechanical.
- Backlogs, waiting times and quality need proper difference-in-differences reporting.
- Few-cluster inference warrants small-sample corrections.
